html:
The Đông Sơn culture was a Bronze Age culture centred on the Red River Delta of northern Vietnam, from about 1000 BCE to the 1st century CE. It is named after a village in Thanh Hóa where its objects were first dug up in the 1920s.

Its people grew wet rice, kept water buffalo and pigs, fished, and travelled in long dugout canoes. They were skilled bronze casters. Their great work is the bronze drum, cast with scenes of boats, feathered warriors, houses on stilts, birds and a star at the centre of the top. Such drums turn up across a wide area, from Yunnan and Guangxi in southern China to Malaysia and eastern Indonesia, which shows how far trade and prestige gifts moved by sea and river.

Vietnamese historians link the culture to the first Vietnamese states known from later tradition, Văn Lang and Âu Lạc, and see it as the root of Vietnamese identity.

Its end came from the north. The Chinese Han dynasty conquered the region in 111 BCE and began a thousand years of Chinese rule. Revolts against it, like that of the Trưng sisters in 40 CE, drew on local pride, and bronze drums kept their meaning long after. Independence came only in 939, when Đại Việt began. Further south, the Cham grew from a different, seafaring culture of the coast.
